title: First-year thank-you list
prompt: Marketing is thanking shoppers in Leeds, Lisbon and Osaka who joined during 2025. Write `solve(customers)` so it returns the `customer_id`, `name` and `city` of the consumer customers in those cities who signed up in 2025.
rules: A customer is on the list when `segment` is exactly `consumer`, `city` is Leeds, Lisbon or Osaka, and `signup_date` is in 2025 (1 January and 31 December both count).
A customer with a missing segment, city or sign-up date isn't on the list.
Keep rows exactly as they appear, duplicates included.
hints: Every rule must hold at once, so join the conditions with `&` and put each one in its own parentheses.
`F.col("city").isin("Leeds", "Lisbon", "Osaka")` checks the city against the whole list in one condition.
A year is a range of dates: from `"2025-01-01"` up to and including `"2025-12-31"`. Filter first, then `select` the three columns.
starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F


def solve(customers):
    # Return customer_id, name and city of the customers to thank.
    return customers
explanation: Four checks must all pass: the segment, the city and the two ends of the year. `isin` covers the three cities in one condition, and the year is `signup_date >= "2025-01-01"` together with `signup_date <= "2025-12-31"`, all joined with `&`. Then `select` keeps the three columns: `customers.filter((F.col("segment") == "consumer") & F.col("city").isin("Leeds", "Lisbon", "Osaka") & (F.col("signup_date") >= "2025-01-01") & (F.col("signup_date") <= "2025-12-31")).select("customer_id", "name", "city")`. Missing values drop out by themselves, because a comparison with a missing value isn't true. The usual slips are `> "2025-01-01"`, which loses New Year's Day, and writing the cities as `==` checks joined with `|` without wrapping them in one pair of parentheses: `&` is worked out before `|`, so the segment and date checks end up applying to the last city only.
